---
title: "Setup"
subtitle: "What to install before the sessions"
number-sections: false
---

You need a working R + Quarto toolchain and an editor. Everything below is standard. If you
already render Quarto documents from R, you are ready.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Setup at a glance
Four steps, top to bottom (each links to its details below):

1. [**Install**](#software) R ≥ 4.5, Quarto ≥ 1.9, and an editor.
2. [**Get the materials**](#get-the-materials) — one line of R, no git or GitHub account needed.
3. [**Install the R packages**](#r-packages) — one `install.packages()` line.
4. [**Check it works**](#check-your-setup) — `source("00-check-setup.R")` from the top folder.

Do steps 2–4 **before you arrive**: walking in with the toolchain already in place means we start on the content, not the install.
:::

## Software

- **R ≥ 4.5.0.** The running dataset (`penguins`) ships in base R only since 4.5 (check with
  `R.version.string`). The exercises use the base-R names (`bill_len`, `bill_dep`, …), so R ≥ 4.5
  is the smoothest path. If you truly can't upgrade, see the fallback below.
- **Quarto ≥ 1.9.** Check with `quarto --version` and get it from
  <https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/>. (1.9 is required: the Typst margin/article layout we
  use on Day 1 landed in 1.9.)
- **An editor with Quarto support** — [Positron](https://positron.posit.co/), VS Code (+ the
  Quarto extension), or RStudio. All work, and we drive Quarto from the command line too
  (`quarto preview` / `quarto render`), so the editor is your choice.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## On RStudio? Check which Quarto the Render button uses
RStudio ships **its own** copy of Quarto, and the Render button uses that one, not the `quarto` on
your PATH. So `quarto --version` can say 1.9+ while the button still runs an older build, and Day
1's Typst margin layout needs ≥ 1.9. Check it in R:

```r
quarto::quarto_version()   # install.packages("quarto") if needed
```

If it's below 1.9, either update RStudio, or point it at your install by setting the
`QUARTO_PATH` environment variable, or just render from the terminal (`quarto render <file>`),
which we do throughout anyway.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Typst (the modern PDF path we use on Day 1) ships **inside** Quarto, so there is nothing extra to
install and no LaTeX to set up.
:::

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
## Stuck on R < 4.5? (dataset fallback)
The exercises assume base R's `penguins`. If you genuinely can't get to R ≥ 4.5, install
[`palmerpenguins`](https://allisonhorst.github.io/palmerpenguins/) and rename its columns to the
base-R names the material uses, so every snippet works unchanged:

```r
# install.packages("palmerpenguins")
library(dplyr)
penguins <- palmerpenguins::penguins |>
  rename(
    bill_len    = bill_length_mm,
    bill_dep    = bill_depth_mm,
    flipper_len = flipper_length_mm,
    body_mass   = body_mass_g
  )
```

Run this once at the top of a document (or your session) before the exercise code. Upgrading R is
still the cleaner path if you can.
:::

## Get the materials

The hands-on files live in a small **exercises folder** (the top `raukr-2026-quarto-exercises` folder):
the starter documents, the reference solutions, and the citation assets (`references.bib`, `apa.csl`).
The easiest way to get it is **`use_course()`** from R. No git, no GitHub account, nothing to unzip by
hand, and the same on Windows, macOS, and Linux:

```r
# install.packages("usethis")   # once, if you don't have it
usethis::use_course("cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises")
```

**What it does:**

1. picks a sensible spot (your **Desktop** by default) and prints where it is about to download the
   files. To
   put it elsewhere, cancel and re-run with a path, e.g.
   `use_course("cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises", destdir = "~/projects")`.
2. downloads a ZIP and **unpacks it for you** into a folder called `raukr-2026-quarto-exercises` (it
   prints the exact path). It then asks *"Shall we delete the ZIP file?"*. Keep it (say **No**): it's
   your one-click reset (see below).
3. **opens the folder** — a new RStudio session, or the folder in Positron / VS Code. If it doesn't
   pop open, open the folder it printed yourself.

::: {.callout-important}
## Which folder to open — and when
`use_course()` drops you in the **top folder** (`raukr-2026-quarto-exercises`). Do the next two steps
(**R packages** and **Check**) from there, now, before the session.

**When the session starts**, open the day folder for that day, **not** the top folder:

- **Day 1** → open **`day1-intro/`** (double-click `day1-intro.Rproj`).
- **Day 2** → open **`day2-projects/`** (double-click `day2-projects.Rproj`).

Each day folder is its own working directory with its own brand and assets, so your renders land
**right next to your files** (there's no project folder above them to capture the output). One
download covers both days. The reference answers are in `solutions/day1/` and `solutions/day2/` at the
top folder. Try the challenge yourself first.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reset without losing work (no git needed)
If an attempt goes wrong, get a **fresh** copy of the day folder (don't unzip over your
working copy):

- **re-run** `usethis::use_course("cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises")`: it makes a new, numbered folder
  and leaves your old attempt untouched; **or**
- unzip the ZIP you kept to a **new** location.

If `use_course()` can't reach GitHub (blocked network / firewall), use the browser: the green **Code ▸
Download ZIP** button on <https://github.com/cderv/raukr-2026-quarto-exercises>, then unzip.
:::

## R packages

The exercises use nine R packages. The simplest path is a plain install into your R library (it works
no matter which day folder you open):

```r
install.packages(c(
  "dplyr", "ggplot2", "gt", "ggokabeito",   # content + a color-blind-safe scale
  "brand.yml", "ggrepel", "prismatic",      # R-side branding for the Typst payoff
  "knitr", "rmarkdown"                      # the engine every .qmd with R code needs
))
```

Or with [**pak**](https://pak.r-lib.org/), which installs the same list in parallel, prefers
binaries, and sorts out system dependencies for you:

```r
# install.packages("pak")   # once, if you don't have it
pak::pak(c(
  "dplyr", "ggplot2", "gt", "ggokabeito",
  "brand.yml", "ggrepel", "prismatic",
  "knitr", "rmarkdown"
))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## There's an `renv.lock` in the folder — ignore it
It pins the versions our CI renders against. It is **not** the participant path: the folder ships no
`.Rprofile` and no `renv/activate.R`, so `renv::restore()` there is not an activated project and
would install its 65 pinned packages straight into your everyday R library. Use the
`install.packages()` line above.
:::

## Check your setup

The exercises folder ships a one-shot check. From the **top** `raukr-2026-quarto-exercises` folder, run:

```r
source("00-check-setup.R")
```

It verifies R ≥ 4.5, Quarto ≥ 1.9, the nine packages, and the base-R `penguins` data, then **renders
the Day-1 Typst sample** (`day1-intro/sample-typst.qmd`). That proves the knitr + Typst chain
end-to-end and **caches the brand's Google fonts** (Albert Sans / Fira Mono), so your first render in
the session is instant instead of pausing to download them. Every line should read `[ok]`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Prefer to check by hand?
The one command that proves the toolchain is `quarto check`. It covers the **knitr engine** too (the
`knitr` + `rmarkdown` packages a `.qmd` with R code needs): it reports your Quarto version and renders a
small knitr test document (look for `Checking Knitr engine render......OK`). If you see
`rmarkdown: (None)`, your R packages aren't installed yet, so do the [R packages](#r-packages) step and
re-run. Then confirm the R side:

```r
R.version.string                          # want >= 4.5.0
"penguins" %in% ls("package:datasets")    # want TRUE on R >= 4.5
```

And pre-warm the fonts once by rendering the sample yourself:
`quarto render day1-intro/sample-typst.qmd`.
:::
